I don't see an obvious quadratic bottleneck in the share apportionment logic, so I'm trying to figure out what's causing the p99 latency to jump from 199ms to 390ms to 1700ms — something must be doing heavy repeated work per request.

Actually rechecking the metrics: error rate is trending down, not up, and only p99 is blowing up while p50 stays fairly flat. That points to a tail-latency issue affecting a subset of requests, not a general performance regression — maybe something like empty-sequence edge cases for accounts with no purchases, though that would typically cause errors rather than slowness.

I'm considering the possibility that only certain accounts are slow, likely ones with large purchase histories, suggesting a quadratic dependence on purchase count somewhere in the summary functions, though the band and category summary loops look roughly linear. I want to make sure the file I'm reading actually reflects what's deployed on main rather than an older indexed commit, and I'm rescanning the code for any place that could scale poorly with history size.

I'm still not finding anything obviously quadratic — the breakdown, category, share, and plain-text rendering functions all look bounded by small constants or simple sorts. So I'm starting to wonder if the latency issue lies elsewhere entirely, or if the file's line count and structure don't quite match what the search results suggested, meaning I should double check for discrepancies in length or content.

The line counts seem to reconcile fine, so that's not the issue. I'm now wondering if the latency isn't from a recursive blowup in statement_sections since it's just called by a few methods normally, and error rates actually declined slightly rather than spiking, which rules out an exception-driven failure path like max() on empty purchases. Maybe the p99 spike is coming from retries somewhere instead.

I'm cross-checking my full list of defs against what I've actually read through, going through each helper function name to confirm nothing's missing—holds, is_empty, net_cents, title, band_for, the category and share summaries, and so on—to make sure I haven't overlooked a hidden function that could be causing the slowdown.

I'm suspecting `purchases_this_month` is the bottleneck since it scans the entire lifetime purchase history and gets called five-plus times per render across the statement, biggest/smallest/mean calculations, and the usual-month comparison. I'm checking other suspects like `band_for`, `_category_summaries`, and category-membership checks, but those all look fine—sets are used properly and nothing else seems to loop expensively.

So the likely fault is those repeated O(n) passes over lifetime history rather than a true quadratic blowup, though I'm not fully convinced that alone explains an 8.5x latency jump. I'm double-checking whether the account page renders all four output formats (HTML, plain text, CSV) each recomputing statement_sections, but those individual calls look cheap since bands are capped at seven, and share apportionment logic also checks out fine.

Since only monthly_statement.py and spend_summary are in scope, the fix has to live there — most likely the render path calling purchases_this_month five separate times (once for render, three for biggest/smallest/mean, once for usual month), each a full history scan. That 5x constant factor on heavy users' full purchase history could plausibly explain the p99 jump from 200ms to 1000ms+ if the scan itself dominates cost.

But actually, the p50 barely moved (178→190, +7%) while p99 exploded (199→1702, an 8.5x jump) — that's the signature of something superlinear in history size, not just a constant multiplier. Five linear passes wouldn't create that gap; small histories should suffer proportionally too. So I need to keep hunting for a quadratic operation, maybe something in the band summary logic that iterates nested over bands and purchases.

Checking through the other candidate functions — none seem to compound across rows in a way that would create quadratic blowup. Maybe the real cause isn't computational complexity at all, but something like retries or exceptions on a small fraction of large histories that only manifest at the tail.

Actually this reconciles cleanly: it's not quadratic, just linear with a heavy constant — accounts with massive purchase histories do many full passes over that history plus this-month data, so p50 (tiny histories) barely notices while p99 (huge histories) balloons to seconds. So the fix is to compute `bought` once and reuse it everywhere instead of recomputing history and this-month purchases repeatedly.

I want to also collapse the band/category grouping into a single pass instead of scanning seven times, cutting roughly twenty passes down to two, while keeping the public function signatures intact so other modules and tests aren't broken — I'll add internal helpers that take the precomputed `bought` value and have the band summary logic build a dictionary keyed by band index in one traversal.

One subtlety: negative-price purchases currently match no band under the filter-based approach, so they're excluded from all totals — but a single-pass `band_for` lookup would incorrectly fall back to the last band, changing reconciliation results. I need to preserve the original exclusion behavior for those edge cases.

Since bands don't overlap, counting into the first holding band matches the existing behavior exactly, so that optimization is safe. I'll similarly convert `_category_summaries` to a single pass with a dict tracking count, total, and refunded per category, and do light single-pass cleanups on the monthly refund/delivery/savings/instalment helpers since those already scan a small this-month subset. The real payoff is eliminating the repeated full-history scans from `purchases_this_month`, which gets called five times plus again inside `_the_usual_month` -- that's where I should focus the restructuring in `render_monthly_statement`.

I'm planning to compute `bought` once and thread it through `_compared_with_usual`, `_biggest_of`/`_smallest_of`/`_mean_of`, and `_the_usual_month`, while keeping the public accessor functions delegating to these helpers so the API stays unchanged. I'm also noting that `as_html`, `as_csv_rows`, `as_plain_text`, and `statement_rows` each redundantly recompute `statement_sections`, including its sorting step, which is another spot worth deduplicating.

For testing, I want a deterministic way to prove the fix rather than timing-based tests, so I'm designing a counting sequence type to substitute for `Account.purchases` that tracks how many times it's iterated, letting me assert the full history is only scanned once or twice per render on a large synthetic dataset.

Writing counting tuple subclass...

I'm tracing through the current code path to count how many times it walks over account.purchases — this-month filtering, biggest, smallest, and mean each trigger a separate pass, plus a length check, totaling five iterations that should collapse to one after the fix. I'm weighing whether to also add a test that catches redundant iteration over the filtered "bought" list within band summaries, though that's trickier to instrument directly.

I'll keep the main assertion focused on verifying a single lifetime scan, paired with correctness checks confirming the rendered statement, reconciliation, band totals, and category totals stay identical to the current behavior. I'm also considering whether the band and category summary logic itself makes too many passes per purchase — right now it looks like seven when it could be reduced to one.

I could restructure the price band lookup so it only reads price_cents once, using a helper that scans the bands by position and delegates the existing holds check to a new price-based method to preserve the API. I thought about writing a test that literally counts price_cents accesses per purchase to enforce boundedness, but that feels too brittle to rely on.

I keep landing on needing a wrapper class that mimics a Purchase but tracks how many times its attributes get read, since Purchase itself is a frozen dataclass and can't easily be subclassed with overriding properties -- so a duck-typed counting stand-in seems like the more workable path for verifying access patterns.

I'll settle on two deterministic regression tests: one asserting lifetime history is scanned exactly once, another bounding per-purchase price reads to 8 or fewer. Then I need to verify my fix actually hits that bound—computing biggest/smallest separately costs 2 reads, so I should look for a way to combine them into a single pass if I want to tighten it further.

Actually, if a purchase falls into a higher band, holds gets checked against every lower band boundary, each involving up to two price reads, so with the top band that's potentially 14 reads alone, pushing well past the bound of 8. So I need my test data to include purchases spanning multiple bands, including the most expensive tier, to actually exercise that worst case rather than accidentally staying cheap by only using low-band purchases.

The real inefficiency here isn't asymptotic complexity — it's a constant-factor blowup from redundant attribute reads per band check. So the honest tests should verify two things: that the purchase history is walked exactly once, and that per-purchase attribute reads stay bounded, alongside standard correctness checks. There's also an existing test file for the spend summary I should look at.

I notice there's an empty stub test for the monthly average calculation, which divides by the number of items bought — that could hit a zero-division for someone with no purchases, but since the test name implies a shopper who did buy something, I'll implement it with a real assertion rather than leave it empty.

Now I'm rewriting the monthly statement module in full, keeping the original docstrings and behavior but restructuring for performance: adding a `holds_price` method on `PriceBand` with `holds` delegating to it, updating `band_for` to use that, and converting the band and category summary functions to single-pass implementations.

I'm also consolidating `_refunds_this_month`, `_delivery_this_month`, `_savings_this_month`, and `_instalments_this_month` into single-pass calculations, adding a `_spread_of` helper that finds the biggest and smallest values in one traversal, and updating `_the_usual_month` and `_compared_with_usual` to accept a precomputed `bought` list so `render_monthly_statement` only computes it once. I need to be careful that the mean calculation still raises a ZeroDivisionError when there are no purchases this month, since that's the documented behavior rather than returning an empty statement.

For `_spread_of`, I'm making sure it explicitly raises a ValueError when the purchase list is empty, mirroring the previous behavior where `max()`/`min()` would raise on an empty sequence, while avoiding an unnecessary list slice copy by iterating through all purchases and tracking the biggest and smallest prices directly.

Now I'm considering the mean calculation — dividing total by count will still raise ZeroDivisionError on an empty list for direct callers, but since spread is computed first in the render path, that check happens before division ever occurs. I also need to verify the single-pass logic for savings this month (tracking discounted savings, count, and total paid) and for instalments this month (outstanding amount and count).

With the implementation plan settled, I'm ready to write out the full monthly statement module including its docstrings, plus a comment noting why the single-pass approach matters for the rollout and tail latency. Then I move to writing the test file, starting with imports from the accounts and monthly_statement modules and building a CountingHistory helper class that wraps a tuple of purchases and tracks how many times it gets iterated over.

I need to be careful here: a generator expression walking through account.purchases only calls `__iter__` once, while `len()` or indexing wouldn't trigger it at all, so the counting logic stays accurate. I also confirm that `purchases_this_month` returns a plain tuple rather than a CountingHistory instance, which keeps the test isolation clean. Now I'm defining a CountingPurchase helper class with fields for price, month flag, category, refunds, delivery cost, discounts, and remaining instalments...

Adding a price_cents property...

For tests, I'm planning one that builds 50 mixed purchases and checks the history is walked exactly once, and another that spans all pricing bands—including purchases over £500 to force a full band scan—verifying each purchase's price is read no more than 8 times.

I'm also sketching correctness tests covering headline totals, count, biggest/smallest/mean, reconciliation, band shares, category breakdowns, refunds, delivery, savings, instalments, and comparisons, plus a test that raises on an empty month. To make these concrete, I'm constructing a small sample account with a handful of purchases across categories (books, groceries, electronics, home) with various refunds, delivery fees, discounts, and instalments, computing the expected totals, and starting to work out how each purchase amount maps into its spending band.

Working through the sample calculations, I confirm the bands reconcile with the headline and category totals, then compute the biggest, smallest, and mean purchase values, refund totals and net after refunds, delivery charge counts, savings share, instalment breakdowns (per-instalment amount, outstanding balance, longest plan), and finally the "usual month" comparison — computing the lifetime average projected over three months versus the actual total, which comes out higher, so the comparison should read as spending "more" than usual.

I'm sketching out test cases to validate this: checking that `problems_with` returns an empty list when everything reconciles, verifying the printed shares sum to 100, and writing a test that expects a ValueError when rendering a statement for an account with no purchases in that period. I'm also considering whether the existing test file needs to be preserved or replaced with actual implementations.

Writing `_band_summaries` logic...

Good, `band_for` stays the same with fallback to the last band. Now I'm building category summaries, tallying counts, totals, and refunded amounts per category from purchases before assembling the CategorySummary tuples.

Then I move to computing refunds and deliveries for the month with similar accumulation loops, and start on savings by tracking saved cents and discounted counts.

Next I sketch instalments logic, summing outstanding balances and tracking the longest remaining plan, then begin the spread function to find the biggest and smallest purchase prices.

I'm rounding out the spread calculation, raising an error if there are no purchases, then wiring up biggest/smallest and mean purchase helpers that reuse this logic before starting a "usual month" comparison function.

Building the usual-month baseline using lifetime totals, then assembling the final statement render with bought items, month totals, spread, and mean values.

I'm checking the ordering of error paths — mean division happens after spread validation, so an empty purchase list gets caught correctly. I've confirmed the lifetime purchase walk only happens once through the boolean check, and the unrelated helper functions stay untouched. Now I'll write out the complete file.
